expected_passages: We classified six languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Russian and Italian) from the VoxForge dataset. VoxForge is an open-source speech corpus which primarily consists of samples recorded and submitted by users using their own microphone.

questions.question: How many samples per language are used, and what is the train/validation split?
questions.ground_truth: 1,500 samples per language, split into 1,200 training and 300 validation (7,200 training and 1,800 validation samples in total)

Out of 1,500 samples for each language, 1,200 were randomly selected as training dataset for that language and rest 300 as validation dataset using k-fold cross-validation. To sum up, we trained our model on 7,200 samples and validated it on 1800 samples comprising six languages.

questions.question: What three models are proposed, and what input does each use?
questions.ground_truth: (1) A 1D-ConvNet that takes raw audio waveforms as input; (2) a 2D-ConvNet with attention (spatial and channel) and a bidirectional GRU that takes log-Mel spectrogram images as input; and (3) a plain 2D-ConvNet, the same as (2) but without the skip connections, attention layers, bidirectional GRU and embedding layer.
expected_passages: Hence, we propose the use of raw audio waveforms as inputs to deep neural network which boosts performance by avoiding additional overhead of computing log-Mel spectrum for each audio. Our 1D-ConvNet architecture auto-extracts and classifies features from this raw audio input.

This model is a similar model to 2D-ConvNet with Attention and bi-directional GRU described in section SECREF13 except that it lacks skip connections, attention layers, bi-directional GRU and the embedding layer incorporated in the previous model.

questions.question: Why do the authors propose using raw audio waveforms instead of log-Mel spectrograms?
questions.ground_truth: Because the log-Mel spectrum must be computed for every raw audio input and its processing time grows linearly with the audio length, acting as a bottleneck. Feeding raw waveforms directly to a 1D-ConvNet (which auto-extracts features) avoids this computational overhead.
expected_passages: As log-Mel spectrum needs to be computed for each raw audio input and processing time for generating log-Mel spectrum increases linearly with length of audio, this acts as a bottleneck for these models. Hence, we propose the use of raw audio waveforms as inputs to deep neural network which boosts performance by avoiding additional overhead of computing log-Mel spectrum for each audio.

questions.question: What techniques enhance the 2D-ConvNet, and what do attention and mixup contribute?
questions.ground_truth: The 2D-ConvNet adds residual/skip connections, spatial attention (to focus on image regions), channel attention (interdependencies among channels) and a bidirectional GRU (for temporal features), plus mixup data augmentation (feeding a linear combination of two random images) to prevent overfitting. The attention+GRU model reached 95.0% accuracy, and applying mixup pushed the 2D-ConvNet to 95.4% for six languages.
expected_passages: We added spatial attention networks to help the model in focusing on specific regions or areas in an image.

We also evaluated our model on data with mixup augmentation. It is a data augmentation technique that also acts as a regularization technique and prevents overfitting. Instead of directly taking images from the training dataset as input, mixup takes a linear combination of any two random images and feeds it as input.

questions.question: What does the misclassification analysis reveal?
questions.ground_truth: The model tends to confuse languages within the same phylum (Romance: Spanish, French, Italian; Germanic: English, German; Slavic: Russian) because they contain similarly pronounced words, and it also confuses French and Russian - even though they are in different phyla - because many French words were adopted into Russian with similar pronunciation.
expected_passages: Our model also confuses between languages belonging to the similar phyla which acts as an insanity check since languages in same phyla have many similar pronounced words such as cat in English becomes Katze in German and Ciao in Italian becomes Chao in Spanish.

Our model confuses between French (Fr) and Russian (Ru) while these languages belong to different phyla, many words from French were adopted into Russian such as automate (oot-oo-mate) in French becomes ABTOMaT (aff-taa-maat) in Russian which have similar pronunciation.
